conflicts.meeting_title: Special Virtual Durham City Council August 27, 2020 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Process Transparency and City-County Fiscal Responsibility for $338,000 COVID Relief Fund Learning Centers Grant
conflicts.summary: Council divided 5-1 on approving $338,000 from the City's $5 million COVID Relief Fund for community learning centers on a late special-meeting agenda, balancing emergency student support against public transparency and county fiscal responsibility.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the $338,000 emergency allocation immediately so 338 students have 11 weeks of learning center support starting September 8, while pressuring Durham County and DPS to assume ongoing responsibility.
side_a_arguments: Students face an acute emergency with the school semester beginning September 8 and doing something immediately is better than inaction.
The County funded six weeks for 338 seats and the City's $338,000 bridges the gap to 11 weeks while the DPS Foundation actively fundraises.
Although public school funding is legally the responsibility of Durham County and DPS, emergency pandemic conditions justify a one-time city contribution.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose approving the expenditure on an expedited special-meeting agenda without prior public notice on a work session agenda and amid disproportionate city-county fiscal burdens.
side_b_arguments: The original funding request and written documentation never appeared on a work session agenda, limiting public transparency before a late-night vote.
The City's remaining COVID Relief Fund is only $5 million, whereas Durham County received substantially more federal CARES Act money and holds statutory responsibility for public schools.
conflicts.resolution: Passed 5-1 on roll call, with Mayor Schewel, Mayor Pro Tempore Johnson, Caballero, Middleton, and Reece voting Aye and Freeman voting Nay.

conflicts.side_a_position: Approve $338,000 in emergency COVID Relief funds immediately to launch 11 weeks of learning center seats by September 8 while emphasizing future funding must come from Durham County, DPS, and private donors.
side_a_arguments: Providing 11 weeks of learning center support for 338 students addresses an acute pandemic need before the September 8 start date.
The DPS Foundation is actively fundraising for the second semester, and partial immediate support is better than leaving students unserved.
conflicts.side_b_position: Withhold support because the funding request bypassed normal work-session public agenda notice and disproportionately taps the City's limited $5 million COVID Relief Fund.
side_b_arguments: The original ask and supporting documents never appeared on the work session agenda and were only placed on a late special-meeting agenda.
Durham County received far greater federal CARES funding and carries legal responsibility for funding Durham Public Schools.
conflicts.resolution: Motion passed 5-1 on roll call (Schewel, Johnson, Caballero, Middleton, Reece Aye; Freeman Nay).

conflicts.meeting_title: Special Virtual Durham City Council Aug 24, 2020 (with closed captions)
conflicts.issue: Ward 3 Finalist Interview Length, Advance Question Sharing, and Candidate Count
conflicts.summary: Council members differed over how to balance meeting duration against candidate vetting—specifically whether to shorten questioning from eight minutes to five minutes, allow PowerPoint decks or narrow the pool from five to four finalists, and share questions in advance.
conflicts.side_a_position: Shorten questioning to five minutes or encourage advance sharing of questions among members and candidates (or optionally cap finalists at four) to keep the virtual interview session manageable.
side_a_arguments: Interviewing five finalists under an eight-minute-per-member format creates a four-hour Zoom meeting.
Sharing questions ahead of time with candidates and colleagues lets candidates prepare concise answers and prevents duplicate questioning.
Reducing interviews to four finalists could also shorten the session if time is the primary concern.
conflicts.side_b_position: Preserve the eight-minute questioning allotment established in prior vacancy interviews and avoid scripting the interview by requiring advance question submission.
side_b_arguments: Council is a deliberative body and must evaluate candidates' ability to engage in unscripted give-and-take on their feet.
Keeping the eight-minute maximum allows individual members to self-regulate and use less time if desired while ensuring sufficient depth.
If questioning is shortened to five minutes, candidates would need PowerPoint presentations to share adequate background.
conflicts.resolution: Council retained all five finalists, kept the eight-minute maximum (with Charlie Reece committing to take only five minutes and the Mayor taking five minutes last), disallowed PowerPoints in favor of three-minute spoken openings, and made advance question sharing optional.

conflicts.issue: Structure of Ward 3 Finalist Interviews (Time Limits, Advance Questions, and Finalist Count)
conflicts.summary: Council members held differing views on shortening questioning rounds from eight to five minutes, requiring or encouraging advance submission of questions, permitting PowerPoint slides, and whether to interview four instead of five finalists.

Sharing questions ahead of time avoids duplicate questioning and helps candidates prepare concise responses.

conflicts.meeting_title: Special Virtual Durham City Council Meeting June 10, 2020 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Neighborhood Protection Overlay (NPO) UDO Initiation Revisions
conflicts.summary: Council split 4-1 (with Caballero absent) on amending the UDO to require governing-body initiation before staff processes neighborhood NPO applications.
conflicts.side_a_position: Adopt the NPO text amendment to set clear expectations on staff capacity and allow Council to weigh in early on NPO initiation.
side_a_arguments: Mayor Schewel noted that NPOs in nearby cities like Raleigh and Chapel Hill have been used to protect privileged neighborhoods and block housing diversity.
Planning staff explained the Old West Durham NPO took four years just to begin due to resource constraints and required years of resident volunteer work without knowing Council support.

Council Member Charlie Reece and Council Member Mark-Anthony Middleton supported the revisions as making the process clearer, though Middleton expressed concern that resource constraints leave no real option outside hiring consultants.
conflicts.side_b_position: Reject the NPO text amendment as an unfair barrier to citizen-led neighborhood protections.
side_b_arguments: Resident speaker Ms. Plass argued the amendment politicizes NPOs before rules are drafted, forces an unfair gatekeeping vote not required of developers, and erodes the only citizen-led tool in the UDO.
Council Member DeDreana Freeman voted Nay on both the consistency statement and ordinance.
conflicts.resolution: Both the consistency statement and NPO ordinance passed 4-1 with Caballero absent/non-voting.

conflicts.meeting_title: Special Durham City Council Meeting May 27, 2020 (with closed captions)
conflicts.issue: Racial Equity in Budget Reductions and New Transportation Financial Manager Position
conflicts.summary: Council members debated whether COVID-19 budget adjustments adequately centered racial equity and flagged the proposed Transportation Financial Manager position for further review against competing city priorities.
conflicts.side_a_position: Insist on deeper racial equity safeguards in cost-cutting and scrutinize adding a new Transportation Financial Manager position relative to other city needs.
side_a_arguments: DeDreana Freeman stated the council must avoid rushing into easy cost cuts with inequitable outcomes ('I can't do a Katrina outcome').
Mayor Pro Tem Jillian Johnson asked to flag the new Transportation Financial Manager position to weigh against all other potential city needs.
conflicts.side_b_position: Highlight equitable transit spending and potential Transit-fund or CARES Act offsets for the Transportation position.
side_b_arguments: Transportation staff noted GoDurham transit expansion is the largest budget increase and serves a ridership roughly 90% people of color, and City Manager Tom Bonfield stated service restoration applies an equity lens.
Charlie Reece pointed out Transportation Director Sean proposed shifting the position from the General Fund to Transit, and Javiera Caballero asked whether CARES Act funds could help.
conflicts.resolution: Staff recorded the Transportation Financial Manager position and Parks and Recreation staffing breakdown as flagged follow-up items with no formal vote.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session July 23, 2020 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Gun Violence Response Priorities (ShotSpotter and Violence Interrupters) vs. Participatory Budgeting Equity Scrutiny
conflicts.summary: During a wide-ranging work session debate following recent fatal gun violence, council members clashed over prioritizing urgent gun-violence interventions such as ShotSpotter and violence interrupters versus repeated critiques of Participatory Budgeting's equity outcomes.
conflicts.side_a_position: Prioritize immediate action and funding for gun-violence interventions—including violence interrupters and testing ShotSpotter—while subjecting all city initiatives, including Participatory Budgeting, to equal equity scrutiny.
side_a_arguments: Addressing gun violence affecting Durham children is far more urgent than Participatory Budgeting.
Children's lives justify experimenting with tools like ShotSpotter, and Council can discontinue it if evidence proves it ineffective.
Council must schedule concrete funding and operational steps for violence interrupters and gun-violence prevention.
conflicts.side_b_position: Avoid conflating the gun-violence crisis with Participatory Budgeting criticism, correct incomplete PB demographic data claims, and schedule a dedicated PB staff and NCCU evaluation briefing alongside advancing the Community Safety Task Force and violence interrupters.
side_b_arguments: Claims that Participatory Budgeting failed its equity goals rely on incomplete demographic data because paper ballots and DPS student votes lacked racial data.
PB staff, the steering committee, and North Carolina Central University produced a full evaluation with improvement proposals that merit an accurate agenda briefing.
Crisis response and expanding violence interrupters should move forward in concert with the Community Safety & Wellness Task Force.
conflicts.resolution: Informational discussion; Mayor Steve Schewel agreed to work with the City Manager to schedule future work-session discussions on both gun-violence/violence-interrupter funding and the Participatory Budgeting evaluation.

conflicts.meeting_title: Special Durham City Council Meeting May 28, 2020 (with captions)
conflicts.issue: Form and Financial Specificity of City Council Outreach to Durham County on Homeowner Tax Relief
conflicts.summary: While all council members favored partnering with Durham County on an expanded long-term low-income homeowner tax relief program, members differed on whether to send a letter citing roughly $1 million, send a letter without a specific dollar figure, or adopt a formally voted City Council statement.
conflicts.side_a_position: Send a Council-signed letter committing roughly $1 million in city funds (or a formal letter without a dollar figure) to invite a County proposal.
side_a_arguments: Charlie Reece suggested a joint letter under all members' signatures indicating readiness to commit around $1 million in administration and grants.
Mayor Steve Schewel supported a Council letter inviting a County proposal at any time during the fiscal year without naming a specific dollar figure because Council lacked consensus on a number.
conflicts.side_b_position: Issue an official voted City Council statement carrying the full formal weight of the governing body rather than an informal letter.
side_b_arguments: Mark-Anthony Middleton argued the issue crossed the letter-writing threshold and needed a formal voted Council statement with the clerk's stamp and raised seal to signal Durham's commitment.
conflicts.resolution: Council suspended the rules 6-0 and unanimously passed Middleton's motion (seconded by DeDreana Freeman) 6-0 to adopt an official City Council statement without a fixed dollar amount.

Jillian Johnson urged immediately deploying the $300,000 already budgeted for Built to Last rather than waiting for the new fiscal year.
DeDreana Freeman warned that relying on existing credit and longevity criteria keeps racial disparities intact and urged equitable relief for struggling cash-flowing businesses.
conflicts.side_b_position: Work with Council, the City Manager, Duke University's $1 million commitment, and a vetted CDFI partner to bring a structured budget and program to the next council meeting for July 1 disbursement.
side_b_arguments: OEWD staff cited administrative capacity, bottleneck avoidance, demographic performance tracking, and NC Exclusive Emoluments Clause legal constraints as reasons to finalize a CDFI-administered loan model for July 1.
conflicts.resolution: Council suspended the rules 6-0 and voted unanimously 6-0 to allocate $1 million to the small business relief program while directing staff to finalize the framework.

meetings.title: Special Virtual Durham City Council August 27, 2020 (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: Convening virtually on August 27, 2020 with all six seated members present, the Durham City Council conducted interviews of the five finalists for the vacant Ward 3 council seat, including opening statements and questioning of Anita Daniels-Kenney on affordable homeownership grants, substance-use policy, equitable engagement, and rezoning decisions, followed by arrangements for a clerk-administered digital ballot ahead of the August 31 selection meeting. At the end of the meeting, Council considered an urgent $338,000 request from the City's $5 million COVID Relief Fund to fund community learning centers for 338 Durham Public Schools students for 11 weeks alongside Durham County's six-week commitment. Council voted unanimously 6-0 on a roll-call motion by Charlie Reece, seconded by Jillian Johnson, to suspend the rules for same-night action, and then approved the $338,000 expenditure 5-1 on a motion by Mark-Anthony Middleton, seconded by Jillian Johnson, with Mayor Steve Schewel, Mayor Pro Tempore Jillian Johnson, Javiera Caballero, Mark-Anthony Middleton, and Charlie Reece voting Aye and DeDreana Freeman voting Nay over transparency, late agenda placement, and county funding-equity concerns.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Spanish Interpretation Setup, and Ward 3 Interview Format
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel welcomed colleagues and the public to the special meeting to interview the five finalists for the Ward 3 City Council vacancy, coordinating with Council Member Javiera Caballero and the City Clerk on simultaneous Spanish interpretation. Mayor Schewel outlined the interview structure granting each finalist an opening statement, up to eight minutes of questioning per council member in alphabetical order, and five minutes from the Mayor.

agenda_items.title: Candidate Interviews for the Ward 3 City Council Vacancy (Including Anita Daniels-Kenney)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Finalist Anita Daniels-Kenney delivered opening remarks highlighting her background in public housing and answered questions from Javiera Caballero regarding budget priorities (proposing homeownership grants for three to five lower-wealth families annually) and policy reforms treating drug addiction as a mental illness rather than criminalizing paraphernalia. DeDreana Freeman questioned her on engaging previously unengaged residents in Northeast Central Durham and resolving community policy tensions, and Charlie Reece asked about past City Council rezoning and annexation decisions such as Guess/Latta Road and a project near Duke; the remainder of the five finalist interviews occurred in the middle portion of the meeting.

agenda_items.title: Digital Ballot Plan for Finalist Selection
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following the candidate interviews, Council confirmed with the City Clerk that a digital ballot listing the five finalist names would be prepared to allow members to vote and have results tallied during the upcoming selection process. meetings.executive_summary: Convening virtually on August 17, 2020 with all six seated members present, the Durham City Council approved the Consent Agenda unanimously 6-0 on a motion by Charlie Reece, seconded by DeDreana Freeman, authorizing a PolicyLink Fines and Fees Justice grant, an FAA RDU Airport grant, eight replacement GoDurham buses for service expansion, a Triangle Land Conservancy Down to Earth Farms watershed agreement, the Discover Durham 'Back on the Bull' campaign, and a $600,000 COVID-19 Public Health Ambassador Initiative shared with Durham County and UNC Gillings School of Public Health. Council then held a public hearing on Item 11 (Cases A1900008 / Z1900023, Farrington Towns), questioning Planning staff Emily Ann Brothers and applicant Jared Edens about why the Planning Commission shifted from an 11-1 approval recommendation in December to a 6-7 failure in June after removal of a wetland retention commitment. Confirming that aerials showed wooded wetland requiring USACE/NCDEQ permitting if filled rather than an unbuffered pond, Council approved the Future Land Use Map amendment, consistency statement, and UDO zoning ordinance across three unanimous 6-0 roll-call votes, before discussing the September restoration of public consent-agenda pulls and work-session public comment.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Pledge of Allegiance, Roll Call, and Council Announcements
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel called the 7:00 p.m. meeting to order, led a moment of silent meditation, Charlie Reece led the Pledge of Allegiance, and all six seated members answered roll call. Mark-Anthony Middleton expressed sympathy for families affected by recent gunfire, a colleague praised DPS educators launching remote learning for 33,000 students, and DeDreana Freeman noted upcoming 100th-anniversary celebrations of women's suffrage.

agenda_items.title: Manager's Priority Updates and Consent Agenda Approval
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Manager noted added info on Item 8 (Down to Earth Farms watershed protection) and placed supplemental Items 13 (Discover Durham 'Back on the Bull' campaign) and 14 (interlocal agreements with Durham County and UNC Gillings School of Public Health for the COVID-19 Public Health Ambassador Initiative) onto Consent without objection. Council clarified Items 13 and 14 totaled $600,000 (not duplicated) with 50% County reimbursement, thanked staff including Aaron Paris on the PolicyLink Fines and Fees Justice grant (Item 3), highlighted eight replacement GoDurham buses (Item 7), and passed the Consent Agenda 6-0.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing — Farrington Towns Annexation / FLUM & Rezoning (A1900008 / Z1900023)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff Emily Ann Brothers presented the Future Land Use Map amendment (Low Density to Low-Medium Density Residential, maintaining the Falls/Jordan watershed overlay) and zoning map change for Farrington Towns, noting the Planning Commission voted 11-1 in December but failed 6-7 in June after the applicant removed a wetland retention proffer. Following questions from Charlie Reece, Mark-Anthony Middleton, and DeDreana Freeman to staff and applicant Jared Edens confirming stormwater review at site plan and federal/state wetland permitting, Council adopted the FLUM amendment, consistency statement, and UDO zoning ordinance in three 6-0 roll-call votes.

agenda_items.title: Restoration of Public Consent Agenda Pulls and Work Session Public Comment
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel and Council Member Charlie Reece discussed restoring residents' ability to pull items from the consent agenda at Monday regular meetings beginning September 8, as well as restoring public comment during work sessions by the end of September.

votes.item_title: Item 11 (Z1900023 Farrington Towns) — Adopt Resolution Amending Future Land Use Map to Low-Medium Density Residential
votes.discussion_detail: Mayor Pro Tempore Jillian Johnson moved and Javiera Caballero seconded adopting the resolution amending the Future Land Use Map for Farrington Towns from Low Density to Low-Medium Density Residential. All six members voted Aye on roll call.

votes.item_title: Item 11 (Z1900023 Farrington Towns) — Adopt Consistency Statement
votes.discussion_detail: Mayor Pro Tempore Jillian Johnson moved and Mark-Anthony Middleton seconded adopting the consistency statement for Z1900023. All six members voted Aye on roll call.

votes.item_title: Item 11 (Z1900023 Farrington Towns) — Adopt Ordinance Amending the UDO
votes.discussion_detail: Mayor Pro Tempore Jillian Johnson moved and Charlie Reece seconded (with Mark-Anthony Middleton also seconding/thirding) adopting the ordinance amending the UDO zoning map for Farrington Towns. All six members voted Aye on roll call.

meetings.title: Virtual Durham City Council Work Session August 6, 2020 (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: At its August 6, 2020 virtual work session with all six seated members present, the Durham City Council opened with constituent updates from Charlie Reece and Mark-Anthony Middleton regarding a Rewood Estates neighborhood development near NC 55 and a 75th-anniversary sister-city celebration with Toyama, Japan, before unanimously voting 6-0 to approve the City Manager's priority items (including a rule-suspension request on a time-sensitive NACTO pandemic streets grant and a closed session on personnel matters). Following review of consent items—including the PolicyLink Fines and Fees Justice grant, eight GoDurham replacement buses, and the Down to Earth Farms watershed project—Council deliberated extensively on supplemental Item 12 establishing the Ward 3 vacancy appointment process. Members resolved questions over whether to fix finalist numbers before applications closed on August 20 by unanimously voting 6-0 on a motion by DeDreana Freeman, seconded by Charlie Reece, to advance three to seven finalists and schedule special selection meetings on August 24 and August 31. Council then voted 6-0 to settle the regular agenda and 6-0 to enter closed session under NCGS 143-318.11(a)(6) regarding conditions of appointing an interim city manager and an employee complaint investigation.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Roll Call, Neighborhood Concerns, and Sister-City Recognition
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel called the 1:00 p.m. work session to order and all six seated members answered roll call. Charlie Reece (joined by Mark-Anthony Middleton) briefed colleagues on a nearly two-hour call with Rewood Estates residents about an adjacent development near NC 55 and celebrated the 75th-anniversary virtual event with sister city Toyama, Japan, while members also praised staff flexibility for working parents and noted a vendor offer for a no-cost six-month technology pilot.

agenda_items.title: City Manager's Priority Items (Minutes, NACTO Grant, Ward 3 Vacancy, Closed Session)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Manager committed to scheduling Middleton's requested items and providing a memo on DPR/Office on Youth after-school and childcare support, then presented priority items: minutes updates (Item 1), a request to suspend rules for same-day action on a NACTO Streets for Pandemic Response and Recovery grant due to an October 1 start and November 1 expenditure deadline (Item 6), supplemental Ward 3 vacancy timeline discussion (Item 12), and a closed session under NCGS 143-318.11(a)(6). Council approved the priority items 6-0.

agenda_items.title: Administrative Consent Items Overview
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Schewel reviewed administrative consent items including the PolicyLink Fines and Fees Justice grant (Item 3, crediting DeDreana Freeman), the Joint City-County Renewal and Recovery Task Force recommendations presentation (Item 4), an RDU FAA Airport Improvement grant (Item 5), eight GoDurham replacement buses for service expansion (Item 7), and the Down to Earth Farms watershed project (Item 8, with a question on whether the $424,000 landowner contribution was a land donation).

agenda_items.title: Ward 3 Vacancy Appointment Timeline and Finalist Process
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council debated how many Ward 3 vacancy finalists to select given that applications would remain open until August 20 at 5:00 p.m., weighing Charlie Reece's caution against locking in a number before knowing applicant volume against DeDreana Freeman's and Jillian Johnson's suggestions for a minimum-maximum range. Council scheduled special meetings at 10:15 a.m. on August 24 and August 31 and voted 6-0 to advance between three and seven qualified finalists.

agenda_items.title: Settling the Regular Agenda and Entering Closed Session on Personnel Matters
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following the City Manager's recommendation grouping Consent Items 1-3, 5, 7-10, updated Item 12, two Recovery & Renewal Task Force items (13 and 14), and GBA Public Hearing Item 11, Council voted 6-0 to settle the agenda. DeDreana Freeman then read and moved a motion under NCGS 143-318.11(a)(6) to enter closed session on interim city manager appointment conditions and an individual employee complaint investigation, which passed 6-0.

votes.item_title: Approve City Manager's Priority Items (Items 1, 6, 12, and Closed Session Request)
votes.discussion_detail: Mayor Pro Tempore Jillian Johnson moved and Charlie Reece seconded approving the City Manager's priority items. All six members voted Aye on roll call.

votes.item_title: Approve Ward 3 Vacancy Selection Process (Advancing Three to Seven Finalists)
votes.discussion_detail: After Mayor Schewel summarized the Ward 3 appointment process moving forward with between three and seven qualified finalists and special meetings on August 24 and August 31, DeDreana Freeman moved and Charlie Reece seconded the process. Mayor Schewel, Jillian Johnson, DeDreana Freeman, and Mark-Anthony Middleton voted Aye on roll call (with Caballero having voiced support for Reece's timeline earlier and Reece's final response falling at the end-of-roll gap).

votes.notes: Mover was not explicitly identified by name in the transcript.
votes.discussion_detail: Following the City Manager's recommendation on Consent and GBA public hearing items, a council member moved and Mayor Pro Tempore Jillian Johnson seconded settling the agenda. All six members voted Aye on roll call.

votes.item_title: Enter Closed Session Pursuant to NCGS 143-318.11(a)(6) (Interim City Manager Conditions & Employee Complaint)
votes.discussion_detail: DeDreana Freeman moved and Mark-Anthony Middleton seconded going into closed session under NCGS 143-318.11(a)(6) to consider conditions of appointment of an interim city manager and an investigation of a complaint against an individual employee. All six members voted Aye on roll call.

meetings.title: Joint City-County Planning Committee (JCCPC) - August 5, 2020
meetings.executive_summary: Chaired by Durham City Council Member Charlie Reece on August 5, 2020, the Joint City-County Planning Committee (JCCPC)—including City Council Member Mark-Anthony Middleton, Durham County Commissioners Wendy Jacobs, Ellen Reckhow, and Brenda Howerton, and Planning Commissioner Brian Busby—began by voting on a motion by Middleton, seconded by Busby, to grant an excused absence to Mayor Pro Tempore Jillian Johnson due to a hurricane-rescheduled work trip. Chair Reece and Commissioner Reckhow clarified prior meeting minutes to reflect that JCCPC had only reviewed a concept memo rather than draft zoning ordinance text on the controversial statutory development agreements text amendment. Planning staff Lisa Miller and Carl Kolosna updated the committee on Comprehensive Plan community engagement amid COVID-19, highlighting socially distanced 'Slow Streets' outreach on Benjamin Street with Spirit House. Later, JCCPC discussed 2017 state statutory limits on requiring developer off-site road improvements in Transportation Special Use Permits—with Chair Reece committing to draft a legislative delegation letter—and reviewed Omnibus 15 UDO text amendments covering TSUPs, Residential Compact (RC) transit-oriented density for future Bus Rapid Transit, RTP public-safety station setbacks, and riparian buffers.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, JCCPC Attendance, and Excused Absence for Mayor Pro Tempore Johnson
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Committee Chair Charlie Reece called the 9:30 a.m. JCCPC meeting to order with City Council Member Mark-Anthony Middleton, County Commissioners Wendy Jacobs and Brenda Howerton, and Planning Commissioner Brian Busby present (and Commissioner Ellen Reckhow participating shortly thereafter). Mark-Anthony Middleton moved and Brian Busby seconded an excused absence for Mayor Pro Tempore Jillian Johnson, whose work trip was rescheduled due to the hurricane.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed (Roll Call; tally truncated in digest gap)

agenda_items.title: Clarification on Statutory Development Agreements Text Amendment Minutes
agenda_items.discussion_summary: In response to Commissioner Reckhow and public emails regarding statutory development agreements, Planning staff Michael Stock confirmed that JCCPC had previously reviewed only a conceptual memo rather than draft zoning ordinance text. Chair Charlie Reece requested that the minutes explicitly note no draft text was presented to JCCPC, while expressing confidence in ongoing Planning Commission and staff work.

agenda_items.title: Comprehensive Plan Update — Equitable Community Engagement During COVID-19
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff Lisa Miller and Carl Kolosna reported on adapting Comprehensive Plan engagement during COVID-19 while managing high development case volume. They highlighted resident outreach working groups, internet and home-environment barriers to Zoom meetings, and socially distanced in-person 'Slow Streets' events led by Spirit House (including Benjamin Street) where residents walked themes painted on the street and recorded goal statements.

agenda_items.title: TSUP Road Improvement Statutory Limits and Legislative Delegation Letter
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following a briefing with transportation staff (Bill) and the City Attorney's Office regarding a 2017 state statute and NCDOT financial constraints affecting developer road-improvement exactions, Chair Charlie Reece stated Durham needs local solutions rather than expecting near-term legislative relief. Chair Reece committed to circulating a draft letter to the legislative delegation after receiving staff details on two affected school projects.

agenda_items.title: Omnibus 15 Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) Text Amendments
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff Michael Stock presented Omnibus 15 UDO technical corrections and policy updates, seeking direction on removing redundant Transportation Special Use Permit (TSUP) triggers for 600+ peak-hour-trip uses where state law bars requiring uncompensated road improvements, updating the Residential Compact (RC) district from light rail to Bus Rapid Transit (20 units/acre), allowing EMS/fire stations in SRP/RTP to use Office & Institutional setbacks, and updating riparian and multi-zoning project boundary buffers. Committee members questioned potential indirect effects on BRT corridor density and asked why recent downtown projects (Geer Street and American Tobacco) did not use the affordable housing height bonus, which staff attributed anecdotally to financing challenges.

meetings.title: Virtual Durham City Council August 3, 2020 (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: At the Durham City Council virtual meeting on August 3, 2020 with all six seated members present, City Manager Tom Bonfield announced his retirement effective September 30, 2020 after 12 years of service, prompting warm tributes from Mayor Steve Schewel and council members. Council reviewed a broad consent slate including the Racial Equity Task Force Final Report, Recovery and Renewal Task Force funding, an employee holiday, transit and water infrastructure contracts, and police grants, with DeDreana Freeman requesting staff follow-up on MWBE/WBE percentage shifts in Items 32 and 33. Following a public hearing, Council voted unanimously 6-0 on a motion by DeDreana Freeman, seconded by Jillian Johnson, to permanently close 89.91 linear feet of Q Place right-of-way to enable two flag lots. Finally, despite public opposition from resident Ms. Plass regarding public engagement and statutory development agreements, Council voted unanimously 6-0 on a motion by DeDreana Freeman, seconded by Jillian Johnson, to approve an expedited hearing request for zoning map change Z1900036 (Farrington Road Multifamily) so the developer could meet an October deadline for 4% Low-Income Housing Tax Credits to build 82 affordable units.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Priority Items, and City Manager Tom Bonfield's Retirement Announcement
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel called the 7:00 p.m. virtual meeting to order, Charlie Reece led the Pledge of Allegiance, and all six seated members answered roll call. City Manager Tom Bonfield reported attachment updates on Items 16, 27, and 45, congratulated Fire, Police, and partners on Safe Kids North Carolina's 'Fit It and Fix It' Program of the Year recognition, and formally announced his retirement effective September 30, 2020 after 12 years as Durham City Manager.

agenda_items.title: Review of Consent Items Including Equity Reports, Audits, Infrastructure, and Grants
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Schewel read the consent agenda covering board appointments, PCI compliance and timekeeping audits, an employee holiday item, the Racial Equity Task Force Final Report (Item 13), Recovery and Renewal Task Force funding (Item 14), Planning FY21 work program (Item 15), transit and parking contracts, water line and utility billing amendments, and police HIDTA grants. DeDreana Freeman flagged Items 32 and 33 for staff follow-up regarding shifting MWBE/WBE participation percentages without pulling them from consent.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Informational / No vote (middle consent vote truncated in digest)

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing — Order Permanently Closing 89.91 Linear Feet of Q Place Right-of-Way
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff, City Manager Bonfield, and City Attorney Kim Rehberg discussed whether Q Place was platted or fee-simple right-of-way and any associated closing fees. Applicant Mr. Blazovich and representative Tom Tiba explained the street closing and lot recombination with neighbor Mr. Henderson would create two flag lots served by common access easements while increasing property tax value; Council closed the hearing and approved the closing order 6-0.

agenda_items.title: Expedited Hearing Request — Zoning Map Change Z1900036 (Farrington Road Multifamily)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Caller Ms. Plass, who pulled the item, opposed expediting Z1900036, arguing it undermined public engagement and invoked statutory development agreements previously barred by Durham's UDO. Applicant representative Dan Jewell explained the proposal provides 82 affordable housing units along a future transit corridor without city subsidy and required an October hearing to apply for 4% Low-Income Housing Tax Credits; DeDreana Freeman, Charlie Reece, and Jillian Johnson praised the unsubsidized 4% LIHTC model while separating the broader statutory development agreement policy review, approving the expedited hearing 6-0.

votes.item_title: Adopt Order Permanently Closing 89.91 Linear Feet of Q Place Right-of-Way
votes.discussion_detail: Following the public hearing with applicant Mr. Blazovich and Tom Tiba, DeDreana Freeman moved and Mayor Pro Tempore Jillian Johnson seconded adopting the order permanently closing 89.91 linear feet of Q Place. All six members voted Aye on roll call.

votes.item_title: Approve Expedited Hearing Request for Zoning Map Change Z1900036 (Farrington Road Multifamily)
votes.discussion_detail: DeDreana Freeman moved and Mayor Pro Tempore Jillian Johnson seconded approving the expedited hearing request for Z1900036 so the 82-unit 4% LIHTC affordable housing project could meet its tax credit deadline, with council members affirming that the separate UDO text amendment on statutory development agreements would still undergo full scrutiny. All six members voted Aye on roll call.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session July 23, 2020 (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: At its July 23, 2020 virtual work session with all six seated members present, the Durham City Council opened with a moment of silence for Durham's 74th COVID-19 fatality, civil rights leaders John Lewis and C.T. Vivian, and 12-year-old gun-violence victim Tom McLean. Council unanimously voted 6-0 to approve the City Manager's priority items requesting rule suspension for immediate action on COVID-19 emergency rental assistance, rapid rehousing, and shelter case management contracts (Items 22-24), and voted 6-0 to approve the City Attorney's closed-session request regarding newly filed federal litigation (Tony Scott Jr. and Tony Scott Sr. v. City of Durham, et al.). Later in the session, members debated how to confront escalating gun violence through the Community Safety & Wellness Task Force, violence interrupters, and ShotSpotter, clashing over Mark-Anthony Middleton's comparison of ShotSpotter scrutiny to Participatory Budgeting (PB) equity metrics—with Javiera Caballero defending PB and requesting a dedicated staff/NCCU briefing while Middleton and DeDreana Freeman urged prioritizing urgent gun-violence interventions. Council concluded by settling the regular agenda 6-0 and voting 6-0 to enter closed session on the federal lawsuit.

agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel opened the 1:00 p.m. work session with a moment of silence honoring Durham's 74th COVID-19 death, civil rights leaders John Lewis and Rev. C.T. Vivian, and 12-year-old gun-violence victim Tom McLean, and all six members answered roll call. DeDreana Freeman announced that the Black Artists celebration was advancing across five community-selected neighborhoods with youth stipends, while Mayor Schewel held the recent gun-violence discussion until after consent agenda review.

agenda_items.title: City Manager and City Attorney Priority Items (COVID Homelessness Contracts & Litigation)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Manager requested suspending the rules for immediate action on three urgent Community Development COVID-19 homelessness and rental assistance items: Item 22 (Durham County CDBG-CV emergency rental assistance), Item 23 (Housing for New Hope Inc. ESG-CV rapid rehousing), and Item 24 (Project Access of Durham County ESG-CV shelter case management), which Council approved 6-0. The City Attorney then requested a closed session for attorney-client consultation on newly filed federal litigation (Tony Scott Jr. and Tony Scott Sr. v. City of Durham, et al., M.D.N.C. No. 1:20-cv-558), approved 6-0.

agenda_items.title: Administrative Consent Items Overview and Planning FY21 Work Plan
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council reviewed consent items, pulling Item 25 (Demand Response Services), Item 26 (cloud parking management), Item 27 (Otis Elevator), and Items 40-41 (2019 and 2020 Police HIDTA grants) for discussion. DeDreana Freeman noted low female staffing representation on Item 28 (Scotty's pressure washing) and praised the equity lens on combined utility billing (Item 34), while Mayor Schewel commended JCCPC Chair Charlie Reece on the detailed Planning FY21 work plan.

agenda_items.title: Gun Violence Response, Community Safety Task Force, ShotSpotter, and Participatory Budgeting
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council members debated next steps on gun violence, crisis response, and expanding violence interrupters—noting DPS agreed to appoint five residents to the 10-member Community Safety & Wellness Task Force regardless of County participation. Tensions surfaced as Javiera Caballero objected to linking Participatory Budgeting (PB) equity critiques to gun-violence debates and requested a dedicated staff/NCCU briefing on PB metrics, while Mark-Anthony Middleton and DeDreana Freeman urged urgent funding and experimentation on violence interrupters and ShotSpotter; Mayor Schewel committed to scheduling future work-session items on both topics.

agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Pro Tempore Jillian Johnson updated her vote to Ashley Ferrell on an appointment, and the clerk noted Recreation Advisory Commission vote totals. Council voted 6-0 to settle Consent Items 1, 3, 4, 6-21, and 25-44 (with Items 22-24 already acted upon) and GBA Public Hearings 45-47, and then voted 6-0 to enter closed session on the federal Tony Scott lawsuit.

disagreements.issue: Gun Violence Response Priorities (ShotSpotter and Violence Interrupters) vs. Participatory Budgeting Equity Scrutiny
disagreements.summary: During a wide-ranging work session debate following recent fatal gun violence, council members clashed over prioritizing urgent gun-violence interventions such as ShotSpotter and violence interrupters versus repeated critiques of Participatory Budgeting's equity outcomes.

side_b_arguments: Claims that Participatory Budgeting failed its equity goals rely on incomplete demographic data because paper ballots and DPS student votes lacked racial data.
PB staff, the steering committee, and North Carolina Central University produced a full evaluation with improvement proposals that merit an accurate agenda briefing.
Crisis response and expanding violence interrupters should move forward in concert with the Community Safety & Wellness Task Force.

meetings.executive_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel presided over the nearly six-hour June 4, 2020 virtual City Council work session with all six seated members participating. Council began with a moment of silence for Durham's 'Butterfly', scheduled a 7:00 p.m. Race Equity Task Force session, accepted the City Manager's priority additions (FY 2021 budget reconciliation and the Durham Small Business Recovery Fund), and reviewed virtual board/commission ballot procedures and upcoming June–July consent and public hearing items. In the final budget reconciliation discussion captured in the digest, Council reviewed six proposed Public Works positions—supporting two general-fund right-of-way safety roles—while Mayor Pro Tem Jillian Johnson questioned preserving a ~16.3–16.7% fund balance rather than drawing it down toward 12%, with staff warning that recurring pay raises ($7 million) would strain FY 2022. Council also previewed June 15, June 24, and July 1 agenda items including the Andrea Harris resolution, DHA and DDI contracts (held pending presentations), GDS Associates carbon neutrality plan, composting and HHW contracts, and planning public hearings (Items 37–47).

agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public Works Director Marvin Williams detailed six requested positions—three fee/stormwater-funded, two general-fund right-of-way safety positions, and one general-fund survey position—with Council voicing support for the right-of-way safety roles. Mayor Pro Tem Jillian Johnson asked why the budget kept fund balance at ~16.3–16.7% rather than suspending policy to 12%, and Manager Bonfield and Budget Director Bertha Johnson explained that using one-time reserves for $7 million in recurring pay raises would create an FY 2022 cliff, though one-time employee bonuses could be weighed while holding the line against tax increases.

agenda_items.title: Resolution of Overlapping Board Ballots and Settling the Agenda
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council resolved an overlapping straw ballot in which Cassandra Stokes received three votes each for the Women's Commission and Housing Appeals Board, shifting a vote so she received four votes for the Women's Commission. Members received annual reports from the Appearance Commission, Board of Adjustment, and Durham Open Space and Trails Commission, emphasizing qualified board recruitment and active trail design. After taking the gavel and apologizing for earlier rotation confusion, Chair Reece nominated BOCC Chair Wendy Jacobs as Vice Chair (seconded by Jillian Johnson); following a parliamentary inquiry by Mark-Anthony Middleton, the committee elected Jacobs 7-0.

Mayor Schewel noted minor corrections to the March 5 minutes and members pulled Items 10, 17, 18, 19, and 20 for discussion ahead of the May 4 regular meeting.

agenda_items.title: Item 10: Contract with Housing for New Hope as Unsheltered Coordinating Agency
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Community Development staff (Karen Lado and Hanaleah Hoberman) answered questions from Mayor Schewel and Mayor Pro Tem Johnson regarding COVID-19 training for street outreach workers, medical partnerships with Duke Clinic and Lincoln Community Health, moving medically vulnerable unsheltered residents into hotels, and Housing for New Hope's expansion to five dedicated program staff.

agenda_items.title: Items 17 & 18: Police District 1 Substation Lease and 1415 W. Club Blvd. Property Sale
agenda_items.discussion_summary: On Item 17 (10-year, $2.9 million Police District 1 substation lease at 915 Holloway St.), Council Member Freeman questioned General Services staff (David Fleischer) on the absence of Office of Equity and Inclusion review for city leases. On Item 18 (sale of a 30x36-foot residual parcel at 1415 W. Club Blvd.), Freeman asked about affordability conditions while Mayor Pro Tem Johnson proposed directing proceeds into the Dedicated Housing Fund and creating a standing policy for future residential land sales.

agenda_items.title: Items 19 & 20: Recycling Processing Contract and Durham County Transit Plan
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Solid Waste staff reported recycling costs swung from $450,000 revenue to over $100/ton (versus ~$40/ton landfilling), while continuing single-stream collection with public education and regional Triangle J coordination. Transportation Director Sean Egan and MPO representative Aaron Cain reviewed the $670,000 Durham County Transit Plan consultant contract and addressed questions from Mayor Schewel and Council Member Freeman about GoDurham's 16-passenger social-distancing cap leaving riders at stops and plans to deploy follow-on buses.

agenda_items.title: Virtual Operations Guidelines for Boards, Committees, and Commissions
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council debated how to allow eager advisory boards to resume work virtually without disadvantaging members lacking internet access, childcare bandwidth, or time during the pandemic, with Reece and Freeman urging caution and Middleton supporting authorizing but not mandating meetings. Council tasked Mayor Pro Tem Johnson and Council Member Caballero with drafting voluntary, no-penalty guidelines using Zoom or Microsoft Teams with tech liaisons and telephone dial-in options.

agenda_items.title: Board and Commission Nominations and Settling May 4 Agenda
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Because six seated members required four votes for nomination, council broke ties via announced vote switches for the Citizens Advisory Committee (Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman), BPAC (Shyla Nappe and Jasmine Joyner), Participatory Budgeting Steering Committee (Cesar Angiano-Ortiz and Shan Almonte), and Recreation Advisory Commission (Cedric Burke), and confirmed Appearance, DPAC Oversight, and Workers Rights nominees. City Manager Bonfield then recommended placing Items 1–4, 6–13, and 17–20 on the May 4 consent agenda, which council approved 6-0.

meetings.title: Virtual Durham City Council April 20, 2020 (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel presided over the April 20, 2020 virtual City Council meeting, the first following Vernetta Alston's departure, with all six seated members present. Council noted expanding written public comment limits from 250 to 4,000 characters, unanimously approved the consent agenda (excluding pulled Item 8) 6-0, and unanimously approved Item 8 (Emergency Response Plan and Source Water Risk and Resilience Plan) 6-0 after remarks from Council Member DeDreana Freeman. Council then held a pivotal discussion on filling the vacant Ward 3 seat after community groups (Durham Committee on the Affairs of Black People, People's Alliance, and Friends of Durham) objected to a 30-day pandemic appointment process. Following legal guidance from City Attorney Kim Rehberg, council voted unanimously 6-0 to rescind the April 6 appointment timeline and voted unanimously 6-0 to proceed instead under N.C.G.S. § 160A-63 (invoked via § 160A-3), eliminating the city charter's 60-day special-election clock and targeting an August 6 work session check-in.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, COVID-19 Update, and Public Comment Process
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel opened the meeting with a moment of silence for 86 residents at a Durham rehabilitation facility diagnosed with COVID-19 and community fatalities, followed by the Pledge and roll call. Schewel noted public comments on loud motorbikes in North Durham and rental distress, announced the written public comment limit was expanded from 250 to 4,000 characters (~500 words), and reviewed Duke modeling showing curve-flattening alongside cautious reopening steps.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Items 1–3, 5–7, 9–23, Excluding Item 8)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council approved all consent agenda items except Item 8 (pulled by Council Member Freeman), including CDBG contracts with Urban Ministries and DHA for Laurel Oaks Townhomes, DHA's McDougall Terrace grant request, Eno River water-supply reclassification support, sewer manhole rehabilitation contracts, the Museum of Durham History lease, Hoover Road Park CMAR amendment, 2019 Q4 crime report, and the Ashton Place Development Loan commitment.

agenda_items.title: Item 8: Emergency Response Plan and Source Water Risk and Resilience Plan
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member DeDreana Freeman explained she pulled Item 8 to commend water management staff for their swift response and planning work. Council then approved Item 8 by voice vote without objection.

agenda_items.title: Rescission of April 6 Ward 3 Timeline and Election to Proceed Under N.C.G.S. § 160A-63
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member Mark-Anthony Middleton argued the pandemic created unequal access barriers for Ward 3 applicants and urged rescinding the April 6 schedule, thanking the Durham Committee on the Affairs of Black People, People's Alliance, and Friends of Durham. Council Member Charlie Reece and City Attorney Kim Rehberg explained that invoking N.C.G.S. § 160A-3 and § 160A-63 avoids the charter's 60-day special-election clock (while leaving the seat open until 2021 if council fails to appoint); council agreed to revisit the timeline on August 6 and voted 6-0 to rescind the April 6 schedule and 6-0 to proceed under § 160A-63.
